newsitem.title: MEXICO: Miners in Mexico dig for colonial leftovers.
newsitem.headline: Miners in Mexico dig for colonial leftovers.

text.p: Miners in Mexico are increasingly scratching around for gold and silver leftovers at old colonial sites rather than trying to locate a new El Dorado.
Turning old prospects that were orginally mined by Spanish conquistadores into new projects is the new vogue in Mexican mining.
One trick to make them viable is using new technology and processing techniques, company officials said here at the Mexico Mining 1997 conference.

For 465 years, the Real del Monte mine at Pachuca has been churning out gold and silver. Now Denver-based Consolidated Nevada Goldfields Corp has bought up the property and has designs on reviving former glories.
President and CEO Geoffrey Hoyl said he will boost output 300 percent in five years.
"At the end of the day, we will be producing 6.7 million ounces (of silver) per year at Pachuca which will make us one of the biggest producers in the hemisphere," Hoyl said at the conference.
Real del Monte has produced 1.3 billion ounces of silver and 6.2 million ounces of gold.
Hoyl said silver output there in 1997 was expected to be 2.7 million ounces, rising to 3.8 million ounces in 1998 and reaching 5.3 million ounces in 1999.
For gold, Hoyl said production would also gradually increase from 13,000 ounces in 1997, to 19,000 in 1998 and 27,000 in 1999.
At Real de Catorce in the state of San Luis Potosi, Vancouver-based Britannia Gold Corp. is starting a drilling programme in February in the silver rich area.

Real De Catorce, now reduced to a ghost town, was first mined in 1773 and production there only halted in 1990 because of low grades and high costs. Over its 224-year history it has produced 200 million ounces of silver.
"We are generally looking at historic Mexican sites," said Fred Felder, mineral exploration consultant for Britannia. "These camps are extremely good ones to explore," he said.

Britannia is on the hunt for around 2 million tonnes of ore in high-grade ranges and has not discounted processing tailings -- leftovers from previous miners -- which total around 2 million tonnes. "Working tailings would not be a primary objective, though," Felder said.
Toronto-based Metallica Resources Inc will revive another gold-silver mine next year at Cerro San Pedro in San Luis Potosi state - a mine that was worked for 427 years.
Louis A. Lepry said plant construction work was scheduled to start in August this year, with output expected between March and June next year.

"We will be pouring some gold in 1998," Lepry said, adding the company objective is to reach annual gold output levels of 150,000 ounces and a silver production of four million ounces per year using open pit mining and leach pad methods.
Over the years the richest veins at San Pedro have been exhausted but there is still enough low grade ore present and within easy access to make the $75 million project feasible.

Lepry said proven and probable reserves above incremental cutoffs were 77.3 million tonnes at 0.6 gramme/tonne gold and 24.8 grammes/tonne silver, which he said worked out to 1.5 million ounces of gold and 62 million ounces of silver.
Lepry anticipated total operational costs of $230 per ounce of gold which still means heathy profits despite the recent slump of gold prices to just over $350 per ounce.
Over the years, Cerro San Pedro produced around 2.5 million ounces of gold and between 40 to 50 million ounces of silver, Lepry said.
Canada's Teck Corp also says its mining strategy in Mexico is to revamp former mines.

"We are into turning old prospects into new prospects," said vice president Joseph Ruetz said. Teck's Mexico unit Minera Teck SA is currently "digging around" at its Nukay gold mine in Guerrero state.
Nukay, although not a mine from colonial days, has been mined for decades.
